newsitem.title: USA: U.S. seeks to revive salmon in northern California.
newsitem.headline: U.S. seeks to revive salmon in northern California.

text.p: Interior Secretary Bruce Babbitt Thursday dedicated a new device to help restore salmon runs in the upper Sacramento River near the Shasta Dam in northern California.

The chinook salmon population in the area has dwindled over the years because dam operations have made the water too warm in the summer and fall for eggs and young fish to survive and too cold in the spring for the salmon to grow.
The $80 million steel structure was designed to control water temperatures by drawing water from many levels of the reservoir, without curbing power production at the dam.
"This is the first time it's being used on a large scale to restore an entire river system," Babbitt said in a telephone interview.

He compared the effort, funded by the federal government, water users and the State of California, to the Interior Department's experiment last year to flood the Grand Canyon in order to restore beaches and wildlife habitat.
"The (Sacramento River) area probably had as many as half a million to a million salmon -- it's down to almost zero now," Babbitt said. "The goal ought to be...to make it return to what it was."

Shasta Dam and Lake are north of Redding, California, at the heart of the Central Valley Project, which handles about one-fifth of California's water and typically generates more than 5 billion kilowatt hours of energy a year.

Installation of the new water temperature device helped to fulfil a 1992 law that required the Central Valley Project to take steps to protect fish and wildlife while also controlling floods, irrigating the area, and producing power.
